How to Spot Counterfeit Precious Metals
Learn essential techniques to identify fake gold and silver coins and bars before they end up in your portfolio.
Counterfeit precious metals are a real and growing problem. Modern fakes are more convincing than they used to be, and a buyer who relies on appearance alone can be fooled. Knowing how to verify authenticity, what tools to use, and which warning signs matter is essential for protecting any meaningful position in gold or silver.
Common Types of Counterfeits
Most fakes fall into a handful of categories. Recognizing the pattern is the first step in spotting the piece in front of you:
Tungsten-filled gold:
A tungsten core with a thin gold shell. Tungsten has a density very close to gold, which defeats simple weight checks.
Lead- or base-metal-filled silver:
Heavier base metals with a silver coating, often used on larger bars where mass is hard to fake any other way.
Complete fakes:
Cheap base-metal blanks plated to look like the real thing. Common for low-value bullion rounds.
Altered coins:
Genuine coins with re-engraved dates or mint marks to impersonate a rarer issue.
Cast copies:
Reproductions struck from molds taken off authentic pieces. Details soften under magnification.
Visual Inspection
A careful look will catch a surprising number of fakes before you ever pick up a scale.
Overall appearance
Color consistency:
Genuine gold and silver are uniform in tone. Patchy or off-color areas suggest plating wear.
Surface quality:
Mint and major refiner finishes are clean and consistent. Pitting, bubbling, or grainy texture is a red flag.
Edges:
Look at the rim for a hint of a different colored metal underneath, the hallmark of a plated core.
Wear patterns:
Real wear is even and shallow. Wear that exposes a sharply different color underneath means you are looking at plating.
Details under magnification
Inscriptions:
Lettering on genuine coins is sharp and crisp. Cast copies look soft and slightly rounded.
Design fidelity:
Compare the fine details (hair, feathers, micro-detail) against a known authentic example or a high-resolution mint image.
Mint marks and privy marks:
Verify the correct placement and style for the year and mint in question.
Edge lettering and reeding:
Where applicable, edge text should be even and aligned.
Physical Testing
Weight and dimensions
A 0.1-gram scale and a digital caliper will defeat most amateur counterfeits.
Weigh the piece against the published spec from the mint or refiner.
Measure thickness and diameter. A tungsten core will usually be off on at least one dimension because of the small density mismatch with gold.
For bars, calculate density from mass and volume and compare against the reference value (19.32 g/cm³ for gold, 10.49 g/cm³ for silver).
Magnet test
Gold and silver are not magnetic. A strong neodymium magnet will not stick to a real piece. On angled silver bars, a magnet will slide slowly due to eddy currents, a useful but not conclusive sign. Many counterfeits also use non-magnetic base metals, so treat this as a screen, not a verdict.
Ping test
Genuine silver coins ring with a clear, sustained tone when balanced on a fingertip and tapped. Gold gives a duller thud. Base-metal fakes usually produce a flat, short sound. The test takes practice and works best when you can compare side by side with a known-authentic piece.
Advanced Testing
💡
When to call in equipment
Visual checks and weight measurements stop most amateur fakes. For larger purchases, or anything bought outside a recognized dealer, ask for or arrange professional testing. The cost is trivial relative to a single bad bar.
Acid testing
Acid kits give an approximate purity reading by reacting with the surface metal. They leave a small mark, only test the outer layer, and are best handled by a dealer who runs them daily.
Electronic testing
XRF analyzers:
Non-destructive composition readings, the industry standard for verifying bullion at the counter.
Ultrasonic thickness gauges:
Detect hollow cavities or core material in bars, which is how most tungsten-filled gold gets caught.
Conductivity meters:
Read the electrical conductivity of the surface. Useful as a screen on silver.
Most reputable coin shops have at least an XRF gun or an ultrasonic gauge.
Red Flags When Buying
⚠️
Walk away if you see these
Prices well below spot.
No honest seller hands you free money. Big discounts almost always mean fakes.
Anonymous sellers on social media, classifieds, or auction sites
with no verifiable track record.
No return policy or no authenticity guarantee.
A legitimate seller will stand behind the metal.
Pressure tactics:
time-limited offers, urgency, or refusal to let you test the piece before paying.
Vague provenance:
“Estate find,” “grandfather’s collection,” no documentation.
Modern Security Features
Many modern bullion products carry anti-counterfeiting features that make verification easier:
Sovereign mint features:
Micro-engraving, radial light-diffracting backgrounds (used on the Canadian Maple Leaf), laser-etched privy marks, and unique textured finishes.
Private refiner features:
Sealed assay cards with serial numbers, holographic elements, tamper-evident packaging, and QR codes that resolve to a verification page on the refiner’s site.
When buying recent-production bullion, sovereign coins and sealed assay-card bars are the easiest formats to authenticate on the spot.
Prevention Beats Detection
The most reliable defense is to never end up with a fake in the first place:
Buy from established dealers with a verifiable history and clear return policies.
Stick to widely recognized products: sovereign coins and major-refiner bars in sealed assays. They are easier to verify and easier to resell.
Keep receipts and any certificates that come with the piece.
If a deal feels off, walk away. A few percent in savings is not worth the downside.
If you want to understand the broader detection toolkit and current counterfeit trends in more depth, see the complete detection guide listed in the references below.
